e.t: Abelmaoula, also rendered Avelmaula, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Kings 19:16. Since no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its exact referent cannot be stated more specifically. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name Abelmaoula itself, with Avelmaula as an alternate rendering.

This noun means “right of kin”: a recognized claim or entitlement belonging to a relative because of family relationship. It describes kinship as carrying a right that may be acknowledged or exercised, rather than merely referring to a family member. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, concentrated in Ruth and appearing once in Nehemiah. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its discussion of family rights.

“Aithalim” or “Ethalim” is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament as a name rather than a descriptive word. The available lexical definition does not identify whether it names a person, place, family, or other specific entity, so its meaning is the name itself, not a general quality or action. It appears once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:53.

This noun means “goatherd,” a person whose work is caring for or tending goats. It names an occupation rather than a personal quality, spiritual condition, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, at Amos 7:14. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: it identifies someone associated with the care of goats. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the sentence in which it appears.

This verb means “exhausted” or “weary.” It describes a person whose strength or endurance has run down, whether physically, emotionally, or under a heavy burden. As a verb, it expresses becoming or being worn out rather than naming the weariness itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalms 142:4. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and prayer, but its central sense is clear: exhaustion and weariness.

Akchō, also rendered Akkho, is a proper name identifying a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or action word, so its meaning is chiefly its role as a name rather than an abstract idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Judges 1:31. The available information does not identify whether the named entity is a person, place, or another specific designation; the surrounding verse would establish that role.

Amari is a proper name, referring to a person named Amari. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it appears once, in Nehemiah 3:2. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text, it does not establish additional meaning beyond the personal name itself. Its precise role in Nehemiah 3:2 must be understood from that verse and its surrounding passage.

This verb means “make dim; faint.” It describes reducing brightness or clarity, or becoming weak and faint. As a verb, it expresses an action or change rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, so it is uncommon in this corpus. Its appearances are in Deuteronomy and Lamentations, but the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “assist”: to help or support someone in carrying out a need or task. It describes an active response rather than merely observing another person’s situation. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Joshua, Esther, Psalms, Isaiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains giving help or support. [p03:word:lxx:L700880:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L700880:occurrences]

This verb means to “call up the dead”—to summon deceased people from the realm of the dead. It describes an act of calling or bringing them forth, rather than simply speaking about someone who has died. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, chiefly in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Joshua. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains summoning the dead.

gl: must be taken up; must be brought
d: must be taken up; must be brought

e.t: This adjective describes something that must be taken up or brought. It expresses necessity: the thing in view is required to be carried, lifted, or brought forward rather than left where it is. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning presents an action as required.

This word means “conduct,” referring to the way a person behaves or lives. As a noun, it names a person’s manner of life rather than a single action. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:23. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular force of the word there, but its basic sense points to observable behavior and the pattern of life a person displays. [p03:word:lxx:L701061:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L701061:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L701061:reference:0]

This word means “repayment”: something given back in return for what was received, owed, or done. As a noun, it names the act or result of returning a due response. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 18 times, showing use across several kinds of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and subject, but the central idea remains a return rendered to another person or received in response to an action.

This verb means “pass by instead,” describing one person or thing going past rather than taking the expected place or action. It presents an alternative movement or course: something passes by in preference to another possibility. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 16:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the act of passing by instead.

This word means “third,” referring to the person or thing that comes after the first and second. It is a noun, so it can identify a third item, person, or position rather than describe an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 45:14. The word itself expresses order or rank within a sequence; its precise reference in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This word describes someone who is exempt from duties—that is, not required to perform assigned service or obligations. It functions as an adjective or noun, identifying a person or status marked by release from such duties. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Kings 15:5 and 2 Chronicles 26:21. Those references show its limited use in this corpus, while the core meaning remains a person or condition free from required duties.

This is a proper name identifying a person called “Aōitēs; Aitis.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:28. The available form preserves the person’s name, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s role in the passage. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identification: it names someone rather than expressing a broader concept.

Barchia is a proper name, also given as Varkhia. It identifies a named person or entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:30. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding text to explain whether it refers to a person, family, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the context of that passage.

This word means “measure.” It is a noun used to name a measure rather than an action or description. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 5:25. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic lexical idea is a measure. It should therefore be understood as identifying a standard or quantity being considered, not as expressing an event, command, or personal quality.

Gabae is a proper name, rendered as “Gabae” and also identified as “Gavae.” It is not presented as a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but as a specific named entity. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 16:6. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that passage cannot be explained further, but its basic meaning is the name itself: Gabae, or Gavae.

Gedan is a proper name, also rendered Yethan. It identifies a person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Judges 20:45. Because names identify rather than describe, its ordinary meaning is the name itself: Gedan. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific person or setting connected with it, but the word’s basic function is simply to serve as a personal or place name.

Gortyna is a proper name identifying Gortyna, also known as Gortina. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a name used to identify a particular place or entity. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:23. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This verb means to adorn something with flowers. It describes the act of decorating with floral beauty, rather than merely referring to flowers themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 1:6, so its normal meaning is clear even though the available record does not include the verse text or surrounding context. The word therefore points to floral decoration, while the exact object being decorated must be understood from the verse itself.

This verb means “pass over.” It names an action rather than a person, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. The word’s precise force depends on what is being passed over and on the surrounding sentence, which is not supplied here. Its central idea remains a movement or action expressed as passing over.

This word is a proper name, appearing as “Dinaioi; Thinei.” It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, at Ezra 4:9. The available information preserves the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain which people or group it identifies there.

This word means “sickle,” a curved hand tool used to cut grain or other standing plants. It is a noun naming an implement rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times, all within Old Testament passages, where its basic agricultural meaning remains consistent. The word can therefore refer plainly to a farmer’s cutting tool, including a sickle used in harvesting or clearing vegetation. Its exact significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to “call out” or “cry aloud.” It describes speaking with a raised voice so that the call is heard, rather than speaking quietly or inwardly. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Kings 4:36. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a loud, audible call. [p03:word:lxx:L704152:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L704152:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L704152:reference:0]

This verb means “dismember”: to separate a body into distinct parts by cutting or tearing. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or inward attitude. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees, including references at 10:5, 10:8, and 11:10. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular scene, but the word itself carries the clear sense of dismembering.

This verb means “exact interest”: it describes taking interest on money that has been lent. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs three times, all in two verses of Deuteronomy 23. Its precise force in any one occurrence depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense remains the act of charging interest.

This verb means “run out,” describing someone or something moving out or rushing forth from a place. It presents the action itself rather than naming a person, object, or condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its recorded occurrence is in 1 Kings 18:16; the precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains an outward movement: to leave or come forth by running.

This adjective means “smallest” or “least,” describing someone or something at the lowest point in size, rank, amount, or significance within a comparison. It can identify what is inferior or lower than others, whether referring to a person, group, or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs seven times, including uses rendered “least.” Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being compared.

Elkōthaim, also rendered Elkothem, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 21:23. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of its name-meaning. Its precise identification and significance therefore depend on the surrounding passage and the person or place being named there.

“Enōb,” also rendered “Enov,” is a proper name rather than a common word with a general action or quality. It identifies a named entity in the Greek LXX corpus, so its meaning is primarily the name itself, not a descriptive idea to translate. It occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:8. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain whom or what the name identifies there.

This verb means “upon,” expressing the idea of something coming on, being placed on, or resting on something, depending on the sentence. It is a concise word of position or arrival rather than a broad description of an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs nine times, so its precise force is determined by what is said to come or be upon something in each passage.

This noun refers to an “attempt” or an “enterprise”—an undertaking or effort someone sets out to carry through. It can describe a deliberate course of action rather than a passing thought, whether or not the effort succeeds. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 9:4, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains an undertaking that a person initiates or pursues.

This word means “say” or “speak,” referring to expressing words aloud or stating something. It is a verb used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings to describe the act of speaking. It occurs 21 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and Judges. Its basic sense remains straightforward: someone communicates a message, statement, or declaration through words. The surrounding passage determines what is being said and why it matters in a particular verse.

This verb describes acting conscientiously: with careful attention to what is right and responsible. It presents a person as taking a matter seriously rather than treating it casually. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs 37 times, so it is a recurring word for this kind of careful, morally attentive action. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word refers to a yoke or to a couple joined together. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it can describe something that links two animals or people in a paired unit. Its central idea is joining or pairing, whether referring to a physical yoke or a matched couple. It occurs 12 times across 12 Old Testament verses, including passages from Leviticus, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Job, and Isaiah.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Ēmasaraim; Imasarem.” It identifies a particular named person, place, or group rather than describing a general quality or action, though the available information does not specify which. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:53. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from that passage’s surrounding text, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a porch or porches—an architectural space connected with a building. Its recorded meaning is “porch to porch?; porches,” so the exact wording is uncertain, but the central idea is a porch or series of porches. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 40:7, in the description of the temple’s structure. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise role there.

Thasiri is a proper name, referring to a particular person or place rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 2:9. Because the available verse text does not accompany this word, its precise referent and role must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context. As a name, Thasiri is not translated by a descriptive English meaning; it is represented by its transliterated form.

This word is a proper name rendered “Iadiēl” or “Iathil.” It identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or doctrine. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles 7:6–11. Because no broader definition or verse text is available here, the name itself is the central meaning; its specific historical role must be understood from the surrounding genealogy in each passage.

Iarbaal, also rendered Iarvaal, is a personal name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Judges 6:32. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying: it names a particular person in that passage. The exact significance of the name in its verse depends on the surrounding biblical text, but this word itself functions as a proper name. This is an LXX Greek entity and should be understood separately from similarly rendered names in other biblical language traditions.

Iethri is a proper name, preserved as the name “Iethri” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:6. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the name’s specific role in that genealogy cannot be explained further without guessing. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply as the personal name Iethri.

This word refers to Jewish speech or language. It functions as an adverb or noun, identifying the language being spoken rather than describing a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, in passages from 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning points to language associated with the Jewish people.

Ioman is a proper name, rendered as “Iōman” or “Ioman.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:19. Because the available information gives the name but not its meaning or a wider word family, it is best understood simply as the personal name Ioman. Its significance in that passage depends on the surrounding genealogy and verse text.

This word means “one by one,” describing people or things taken individually rather than all together. It functions as a number expression, emphasizing separate members in a sequence or group. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:34. The surrounding verse is needed to show exactly how the expression functions in that sentence, but its basic sense is clear: each person or thing is considered separately, in turn. [p03:word:lxx:L706994:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L706994:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L706994:reference:0]

This adjective describes something that bears fruit or is productive—“fruit-bearing; fruitful.” It can describe a tree, plant, or anything characterized by producing fruit. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures. Its basic sense is straightforward: it points to fruitful productivity rather than barrenness. The surrounding verse determines whether the word refers literally to plants or uses fruitfulness as a descriptive comparison.

καταπαίζω is a verb meaning to mock at someone—to ridicule or scorn them rather than speak of them neutrally. It describes an act of derision directed toward a person. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times, in two books: 2 Kings and Jeremiah. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on surrounding context, but its basic sense is the act of mocking.

Keila, also rendered Kila, is a proper name identifying a person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage, but the name itself does not express a general concept or command. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs 17 times, appearing especially in 1 Samuel and also in 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah. This is a Greek LXX name and should not be treated as a general English vocabulary term.

Keneroth is a proper name, rendered “Keneroth,” rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs only once, in Joshua 11:2. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name and its location in the text are clear, but its specific role in that verse is not. It should therefore be read as a name, not translated as a general concept or attribute.

Koreim, also given as Korim, is a proper name identifying a particular named figure or entity rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This LXX word occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 26:1. Since the available information provides the name and its location but not the verse text or surrounding details, its specific identity and role must be understood from that passage. The name itself functions as a designation, not as a general word with an ordinary descriptive meaning.

Krates is a proper name identifying a person, rendered here as “Kratēs” or “Kratis.” It is not presented as a general noun, action, quality, or theological term, so its meaning is primarily its role as a personal name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:29. Without the verse text, no further claim can be made about the individual or the significance of the name in that passage.

The word means “marble,” a noun for the hard, smooth stone used as a material. It identifies a physical substance rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Epistle of Jeremiah 1:71. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, that reference does not by itself establish how the stone functions in the sentence; the secure lexical sense remains the stone itself.

This word means a mediator: a person who stands between others to help address a division or bring them into agreement. It is a noun, so it names such a person rather than describing an action or quality. The central idea is someone positioned between parties. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Job 9:33. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains mediator.

This word means “hatred of wickedness.” It is a noun describing an attitude of rejecting what is wicked, not merely recognizing it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:1. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: opposition toward wickedness expressed as hatred.

Mooli is a proper name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named individual within genealogical and family records. Its meaning is therefore the name itself: “Mooli.” The name occurs 13 times across 12 verses, appearing in Exodus, Numbers, 1 Chronicles, and Ezra. Without the surrounding verse text, no further personal description or significance should be assigned to the name.

Nathan is a proper name—the personal name Nathan, rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it appears 47 times and is consistently rendered “Nathan.” The name occurs in passages spanning Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Sirach, so its normal function is to identify a person. The particular Nathan intended in any verse must be determined from the surrounding passage.

This word refers to childhood or childishness—the state or character associated with being a child. As a noun, it can describe an early stage of life or behavior marked by childlike immaturity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Ezekiel and Hosea. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its comparison with the person’s later conduct.

This word describes something connected with law or a person concerned with legal matters—a “lawyer.” It functions as an adjective, so it identifies a legal role or quality rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:4. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the emphasis there falls on the person’s legal role or on something characterized as legal.

This noun means “shaving,” referring to the removal or cutting of hair. It names the act itself rather than a person, place, or inner quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 22:12. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its precise role in that passage cannot be described further; however, its ordinary meaning remains the act of shaving. [p03:word:lxx:L709432:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L709432:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L709432:reference:0]

This Greek LXX adjective means “few” or “sparse,” describing a small number or limited amount. It can refer to people, things, or portions, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs 94 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it commonly expresses the idea of scarcity or smallness rather than abundance. Its precise application depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This adjective describes people who agree with one another or share the same mind. It can refer to unity of thought or agreement between persons, rather than merely describing someone’s private opinion. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Susanna 1:60. The word’s central idea is harmony: those described by it are in agreement with each other. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how that agreement functions in its particular setting.

This Greek LXX verb means “sharpen”: to make something keener, more pointed, or better prepared for cutting. It is used for the action of sharpening an object, especially a weapon or tool, rather than naming the object itself. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with several uses in Ezekiel describing a sharpened sword. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains making something sharp and ready for use.

This word expresses “woe”—a cry of distress, grief, or warning about serious trouble. It functions as an interjection or noun, drawing attention to a condition that brings misery or calls for lament. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 64 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion of the corpus, and appears especially often in Isaiah and Jeremiah. Its repeated use shows that “woe” can mark both sorrow over painful circumstances and a solemn announcement of coming trouble. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “miscalculate” or “defraud”: to reckon something wrongly or deal dishonestly with another person. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times, including passages from Genesis, Joshua, Samuel, Esther, and Bel and the Dragon. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is mistaken calculation or deliberate deception, but both senses involve treating a matter inaccurately or unfairly.

This verb means “lapse” or “fall away”: it describes turning aside from a position, course, or standing rather than remaining in it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, chiefly in Ezekiel, with additional occurrences in Esther and Wisdom. Its central idea is movement away—a departure, failure, or falling from what was previously held or followed. The exact force in any verse comes from its surrounding passage.

This noun means a bridal chamber—the room associated with a bride and groom. It can be rendered more generally as a chamber when the surrounding context does not emphasize the wedding connection, but its central sense is a room prepared or used for marriage. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Psalms, Joel, and 3 Maccabees. Its exact significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “flat,” describing land or a place as level rather than raised or steep. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings to identify terrain and regions by their physical character. The word occurs 20 times in this Greek LXX corpus, mostly in Old Testament books, so its normal sense remains a straightforward description of level ground. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “turn about” or “divert,” describing a change in direction or the act of turning something aside. It expresses movement away from a present course, whether by turning around or redirecting something. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 5:23. Since the verse text is not provided here, the precise force of the word in that passage must be determined from its surrounding context.

This noun refers to someone or something that is near or close to another person or thing. It describes nearness or proximity rather than distance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Song of Songs 5:1. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: a person or thing nearby, close at hand, or near another.

This noun means an old woman: a female person advanced in age. It identifies the person by age and sex rather than describing an action, feeling, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:14. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here; its basic lexical meaning remains simply “old woman.”

This Greek Old Testament verb means “attach oneself to someone.” It describes joining or associating oneself with another person, rather than merely being nearby. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Leviticus and Numbers. Its basic sense is personal connection: one person becomes associated with another. The surrounding passage determines whether that attachment is temporary, relational, or connected with participation in a group or activity.

This noun means “attention”: focused notice given to something or someone. It describes the act of directing the mind toward a matter rather than overlooking it. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word names an attentive response or careful regard, while the particular object receiving attention must be understood from each passage’s context.

This noun refers to a prince or ruler—someone who holds authority over others. It names a person according to position and leadership rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:2. The word’s basic sense remains focused on an elevated human authority, such as a governing leader or prince. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “fire” or “refine.” It describes the action of exposing something to fire, whether literally or as a refining process that tests and purifies. The word appears 24 times across 22 verses in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic idea is repeated in several settings rather than limited to one passage. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and context. The LXX usage includes references in 2 Samuel, Esther, Psalms, Proverbs, Zechariah, and the Maccabean books.

This word means “drop,” referring to a small amount of liquid. It is a noun, so it names the drop itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, in Wisdom 11:22. That single occurrence establishes its ordinary sense but does not, by itself, explain the full thought of the verse without the surrounding text. The word therefore carries a simple, concrete meaning: one drop or a small quantity of liquid.

Rachel is a personal name, referring to the woman named Rachel in the Old Testament. It functions as a noun rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears 50 times across 47 verses, with most occurrences in Genesis, where Rachel is a prominent person in the family history of Jacob. The name also appears later in Ruth, 1 Samuel, and Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies Rachel.

This word means “flow,” referring to something that runs or pours out. It is a noun, so it names the flow itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 19 times, with most occurrences in Leviticus 15. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains a flowing or running out. The word is also found in Deuteronomy, Job, and Sirach.

This word is a proper name, identifying someone called “Sēa” or “Sia.” It is not a general description or action word, but a personal name used to distinguish an individual in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Nehemiah 7:46. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding list and context, but its basic meaning is the name itself rather than an added quality or activity.

This noun means an allowance of wheat: a measured or provided supply of grain. It refers to wheat given out for someone’s needs rather than to wheat in general. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis 42, where the surrounding passage concerns provisions of grain. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a provided quantity of wheat.

This adjective describes someone or something as diligent—careful, earnest, and committed to doing what is required. It points to purposeful effort rather than laziness or neglect. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Ezekiel 41:25, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains steady, focused effort. As an adjective, it describes a person, action, or quality marked by diligence rather than naming the effort itself.

This noun means “socket”: a fitting or receiving part designed to hold another piece in place. It refers to a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Kings and once in 1 Chronicles. The precise object being described depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains a socket or fitted receptacle.

This noun means “interpretation”—the explanation or making known of what something signifies. It refers to the act of giving understandable meaning, especially when a message, dream, or saying needs to be explained. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 22 times, with uses recorded from Genesis through Wisdom. Its clearest English rendering is “interpretation,” and the word should be understood broadly as the explanation of meaning rather than as the message or thing being interpreted itself.

This verb means to live with someone, describing shared life or residence. It presents living together as an ongoing action rather than a single meeting or brief visit. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 13:5, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The basic idea remains a person dwelling or associating together with another. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus, distinct from Hebrew and Greek New Testament source words.

This verb means “grow together,” describing living things or parts developing alongside one another as a connected whole. It focuses on shared growth rather than merely becoming larger independently. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Because the actual verse wording and surrounding passages are not included, the precise subject and force in each occurrence must be determined from its context.

This verb means “condense”: to make something more compact, closely gathered, or concentrated. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, across Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and 1 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being brought together or made compact there, but its central idea remains the drawing together or tightening of something. This adjective describes someone or something as wretched—that is, in a miserable or pitiable condition. It is a descriptive word rather than a name or action, and it characterizes a person or thing in negative terms. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including Psalms and several Wisdom and Maccabees passages. Taphou, also rendered Tafu, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. Its precise referent depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the name itself does not describe an action, quality, or doctrine.

This Greek LXX word describes someone or something as “thrice-sinful” or “thoroughly evil.” As an adjective, it intensifies the description of serious wickedness; as a noun, it can refer to a person characterized by that evil. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Esther and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning is strongly negative: extreme or deeply established evil.

This verb means to “lie under,” describing something positioned beneath something else. This word means “later”. It is an adverb, so it points to something that happens or is considered after another time or event. In the Greek Scriptures represented here, it occurs fifteen times. This adjective means “foul,” describing something as unpleasant, bad, or offensive in the setting where it appears. Its basic force is descriptive rather than naming a person or action. This noun means “love of honour”: an expressed regard for honour as something valued or sought. It identifies an attitude or desire rather than an action itself. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central idea remains love directed toward honour.

This adjective describes someone as cherishing—showing warm, devoted affection toward another. It expresses a caring attitude rather than naming a person, place, or action. This noun means “bark,” the outer covering of a tree or woody plant. It names the material found on the outside of a tree rather than the inner wood. This verb means to levy tribute from someone—that is, to require a payment or tax from them. It describes the act of collecting tribute rather than the tribute itself. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a demand for tribute or payment.

Charadath, also identified as Kharathath, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a specific name. The available information identifies the name and its occurrences but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain further details about the place or its significance.

This Greek LXX verb means “subdue” or “attack”: it describes acting against someone or something with force, either to overcome it or to assault it. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The exact force—overpowering or attacking—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage.

Chrysolite is the name of a precious stone. In the Greek Old Testament, it is treated as a noun naming a particular gemstone rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word occurs three times in this corpus: twice in Exodus and once in Ezekiel. Its exact appearance, color, or symbolic significance is not stated by the word itself; those details would require the surrounding verse and passage. This Greek LXX verb means “testify falsely”: to give testimony that is untrue, especially in a legal or witness setting. It describes dishonest speech presented as evidence against another person, rather than a simple mistake or misunderstanding. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus 20:16 and Deuteronomy 5:20, both within the wording of the command against false testimony. Its precise force in either verse is understood from the surrounding command and passage.
